1-HOUR DIGEST

Fabulous Adventures in Data Structures and Algorithms

by Eric Lippert · Manning Publications

Not the undergraduate canon — no balancing trees, no sorting arrays. This is the off-the-beaten-path material Lippert had to learn on the job, mostly from research papers: persistent structures, finger trees, Gosper's HashLife, DAWGs, unification, and a Bayesian probability library, all built in C# around one theme — immutability you can exploit.

  • ≈ 60 min read
  • ≈ 11,000 words
  • 25 figures from the book (+cover)
  • 1 through-line project: Fabulous.Collections (Python)

What you'll learn

  1. Why immutable, persistent data structures make whole classes of bugs impossible — and how covariance, free undo-redo, and O(1) list reversal fall out of them.
  2. How end-buffer chunking builds a finger tree with O(log₃ n) worst-case deque operations, and how memoized quadtrees compute trillions of Life generations in seconds.
  3. How DAWGs, graph coloring, pretty printers, and Robinson unification power real developer tools — with the exact numbers.
  4. The monad pattern, from Nullable<T> to LINQ to a full probability monad that automates Bayes' theorem.
  5. How to sample any distribution: the alias method, inverse transform, rejection sampling, and Metropolis — ending in continuous Bayesian posteriors.
How to read this digest. Word and time chips are honest and derived from this file itself: the total counts all visible body text — prose, figure captions, tables, chips, and takeaways — excluding code blocks, divided by 230 words per minute, with each of the 25 figures adding roughly half a minute. Per-chapter budgets are ≤700 words (interludes ≤550). Code cards quote the book's C# implementations (condensed where marked); the runnable through-line project named on each card is Python, fully tested on this machine. Image placeholders are inlined with the book's own figures at build time. Companion code: github.com/EricLippert/FabulousAdventures.

INTRODUCTION

Why this book is fabulous

Eric Lippert spent years on the Microsoft teams behind the C# compiler, its IDE, and developer tooling; the book is kindred to his long-running blog (ericlippert.com). Its opening chapter asks what earns a data structure the word "fabulous," and answers with a nine-point taxonomy that secretly is the table of contents:

  1. Solving a real problem off the beaten path — anti-unification, to find common patterns in thousands of code changes.
  2. Achieving a counterintuitive result — the best undo-redo is built from data that cannot change.
  3. Applying one solution across many domains — backtracking finds items, colors maps, solves Sudoku, formats code.
  4. Emphasizing meanings, not mechanisms — probability code that reads like probability.
  5. Looking like a magic trick — the Hughes list, a "linked list" that appears to contain no data at all.
  6. Taking full advantage of a language feature — a recursive generic type impossible in C++ templates.
  7. Challenging the frame, changing the game — Gosper's HashLife, a grid of bits reimagined as an immutable quadtree.
  8. Connecting with theory — category-theory interludes that explain why C# says out T and in T.
  9. Having fun! — Lippert has programmed since age nine, on a Commodore PET.

The through-line is persistence. Because immutable structures never change, new versions reuse their internals, so "old" states stay alive for free — which is what makes undo-redo trivial, backtracking cheap, memoization legal, and (by the last chapter) Bayesian inference over continuous distributions a dozen lines of code. To make that arc visible, this digest materializes the book's sample code as one growing library, Fabulous.Collections — the cards quote the book's C#, and the complete library ships as a fully tested Python package; every chapter ends with its increment, and the closing section shows the complete tree.

Part 1 · Chapters 1–7

Extending the basics

Traditional structures with a twist: persistence, memoization, "a truly bizarre way to reverse a linked list in seemingly constant time" — plus a detour into the category theory that explains it all.

CHAPTER 1

Starting a fabulous adventure

An algorithm is a finite sequence of steps that solves a problem; a data structure organizes information. "Solving problems using organized data is what computer programming is all about." Crucially, algorithms need not be deterministic, computer-executed, or even clever — but their complexity, the relationship between problem size and cost, must be understood.

Big O notation (named by Paul Bachmann in the late 19th century; "algorithm" itself comes from the 9th-century Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi, who also gave us "algebra") sorts costs into a ladder: constant, logarithmic ("so slow-growing they're almost never the bottleneck"), linear, quasilinear, quadratic, exponential, factorial. Problems where every algorithm is exponential or worse are intractable. The ladder's most dangerous rung is the one you fall into by accident: naïve string concatenation with s += x copies the string every time — accidentally quadratic, O(n²) in both time and memory where a StringBuilder gives O(n).

⚠ Lippert's warning. As a Visual Basic team intern he flagged an O(n²)-worst-case string search — and was patiently told that scalability matters only when problems get big; VB users search short strings, where the naïve method is blazingly fast. "If problems are always small, asymptotic complexity matters less." Cost also isn't only time: memory, and best- vs average- vs worst-case time (chapter 2 adds amortized) all count.

The warm-up is a recursive definition — "a linked list is either empty or a value followed by a tail linked list" — as a C# record with an Empty singleton, then a self-critique in the author's signature style: representing emptiness with nulls lets you build invalid lists; "ideally, it should be hard or impossible to create an object in an invalid state" (chapter 2's null object pattern fixes this). And the first hidden cost of generated code: records synthesize recursive value equality, so an innocent IsEmpty check can overflow the call stack on a long list.

The chapter closes with his 1996 Microsoft interview: asked to reverse a linked list, he pushed each node onto the empty list. Because the list is immutable, the original survives untouched; the cost is O(n) time and O(n) extra memory. File it away — chapter 2 does it in "constant" time.

Takeaways

  • Complexity = size vs cost; the ladder is about steepness, and "accidentally quadratic" is the rung to fear.
  • Better asymptotics isn't automatically better — measure, and know your input sizes.
  • Immutable lists are easy to reverse non-destructively; record-generated equality is a hidden stack-overflow hazard.

CHAPTER 2

Immutable stacks and queues

"The less things change, the more they stay the same": any fact deduced about an immutable object stays true forever. When Microsoft rebuilt the C# compiler as Roslyn, the team deliberately biased itself toward immutable structures — "and whole classes of bugs became impossible" (a fact cached, the structure mutated, the fact used).

Banks keep append-only ledgers, not mutable balances; validated data is frozen in flight to defeat TOCTOU races between check and use; immutable objects cross threads without locks; and immutability buys memoization (time: cache pure-function results) and persistence (space: new versions reuse internals).

Methodologically, stop designing containers and start designing abstract data types: what operations do users want, which values are legal? The stack falls out as IImStack<T> with a null-object EmptyStack singleton — emptiness is a valid object, never null, and the only way to build a stack is Push — all four operations O(1).

Then the covariance trick. Mutability breaks variance: convert IList<Tiger> to IList<Animal>, Add a Giraffe, and a Tiger variable reads a Giraffe. So mutability prevents covariance; C# allows out T only in output positions. Push(T) takes T as input, which would forbid covariance — so move it out of the interface into an extension method, making IImStack<out T> legal and safe. "I don't often see this technique used." (The theory arrives in chapter 7.)

The two-stack queue keeps an enqueues stack and a dequeues stack; when the latter empties, reverse the former into it — chapter 1's Reverse, finally paying rent. Its invariant: every nonempty queue has a nonempty dequeue stack (enqueuing onto an empty queue writes straight onto the dequeue stack — "code we don't have to write is bug-free code!"). Enqueue is O(1); Dequeue is worst-case O(n) but amortized O(1): every item is pushed twice and popped twice. Lippert then flags his own argument's flaw — undo can repeat the expensive operation at will, so the amortization breaks. Mitigations: don't worry; a worst-case-cheap deque (chapter 3); or memoized reversal (chapter 4). Deep dive: Okasaki, Purely Functional Data Structures (1999).

Undo-redo becomes a wrapper: UndoRedo<T> holds the current state plus stacks of whole states. Persistence makes each undo entry O(1) on average — and redo is free even when the original operation was O(n), which command-pattern implementations don't get.

The finale is the Hughes list (John Hughes; aka the difference list): a struct whose only field is a single Concat delegate. Empty is the identity function; Push, Append and Concatenate merely compose functions — O(1) to build; Peek, Pop, and enumeration force ToStack() — O(n). Compiled lambdas reveal the trick: each closure "closely resembles a node of a binary tree," so a Hughes list is secretly a binary tree of closures — and a few thousand appends consume O(n) call stack on realization. The punchline: Reverse is O(1) to construct. "The next time an interviewer tells you to reverse a list, tell them that if you can use a Hughes list, you can do it in O(1) regardless of the size of the list being reversed. See whether they tell you that's wrong." (Realizing it still costs O(n).)

Takeaways

  • Memoization (time) and persistence (space) are distinct wins of immutability; Roslyn bought entire bug classes with it.
  • Two-stack queue: worst-case O(n), amortized O(1) — and undo breaks the amortization.
  • Demote mutating ops to extension methods and even stacks get covariance.
  • Hughes list: O(1) build, O(n) read; secretly a tree of closures.

CHAPTER 3

An immutable deque

A deque needs cheap add/remove at both ends, and "it's not clear how to implement this efficiently." A finger tree keeps designated nodes — the fingers — cheap to reach by keeping them close to the root; here, the leftmost and rightmost items. Third goal: real concatenation, where the Hughes list's O(1) "is a bit of a cheat because all it does is make a function that performs the O(n) concatenation later"; this chapter concatenates in genuinely sublinear time.

The first attempt is a deliberate strawman: "a deque is empty, a single item, or a left item followed by a deque followed by a right item." Every push shifts the old end item into the middle, rebuilding the whole spine — O(n) allocation per operation. "This data structure isn't persistent at all," and its recursive enumerator is worse: O(n) stack depth and O(n²) time. It's easy to accidentally design an immutable structure that works but lacks the persistence required to be efficient.

The fix keeps the shape — ends plus an overflow-absorbing middle — but makes overflow rare. Each end gets a mini-deque of one to four items (IMini: records One–Four, no empty state; sized 4 because that's all the tree needs). The new definition: "a deque of items is an empty deque, a single item, or a left mini followed by a middle deque of minis followed by a right mini." When a Four overflows, three items leave as a Three and the middle — a deque of minis — recursively chunks chunks of chunks.

The amortized analysis is beautiful: 2 of every 3 pushes touch only level 1, 2 of 9 touch two levels, 2 of 27 three — 2 of every 3d cost d levels, so the worst case happens "only about twice" in n pushes. Any push/pop is worst-case O(log₃ n) time and extra space, amortized O(1); a d-deep tree of Threes holding 3d items adds only (3d−1)/2 overhead objects — under half the payload. Absent: any tree-balancing invariants, red-black-style. And recursion depth is only O(log₃ n), so the call stack never overflows, even for billions of items.

The type-system marvel: each level's middle holds a larger type — Deque<char>, then IDeque<Deque<char>.IMini>, then deeper — an infinitely growing generic type. C++ templates expand every instantiation and "these sorts of infinitely growing types can indeed create havoc"; C# and Java have genuinely generic runtimes that reuse generated code. "This data structure changed the way I think about generics."

Concatenation then weakens the invariant: the middle may hold Twos as well as Threes (never a chunk of one). Each mini learns TwosAndThrees (a switch over all 16 pairwise cases); two multi-item deques merge their inner ends into Twos/Threes, push them onto the left's middle, and recurse on the middles. Cost: at most O(log n) steps of amortized-O(1) work — worst-case O(log n), genuinely cheap where Hughes deferred. The price: worst-case depth degrades to O(log₂ n), and bad cases shift from 1-in-3 to 1-in-2 pushes. Finger trees began as a B-tree improvement (size tracking also yields priority queues and interval trees), but the takeaway is the heuristic: solve a much more restricted problem straightforwardly, then build the elegant solution on it.

Takeaways

  • Plausible recursion can silently destroy persistence: O(n) per op, O(n²) enumeration.
  • Exact complexity: amortized O(1), worst case O(log₃ n) (O(log₂ n) after weakening), O(log n) real concatenation.
  • Chunking buys a shallow tree with no balancing invariants; growing generic types are safe in C#, havoc in C++.

CHAPTER 4

Memoizing immutable quadtrees to make a better Life

Conway's Life — "not really a game: although it has rules, it has no players" — is born with three neighbors, survives with two, dies otherwise; it has still lifes, the blinker oscillator, the glider spaceship, and is Turing-complete. Lippert wrote it as a teenager on a Commodore 64 and Amiga 500; here it becomes the vehicle for HashLife, Bill Gosper's 1980s algorithm, which "illustrates better than any other algorithm I know" the chapter's two-paths thesis: incrementally improve hot spots, or challenge your frame of reference.

Path one is measured. BoolArrayLife: two 258×258 byte[,] grids swapped per tick (bytes benchmarked faster than bools — "there's no substitute for measurement"), O(n) per tick, about 1,200 ticks/second. SIMD buys ≈10×, a GPU ≈200× — "excellent," but the algorithm is still O(n) per tick. The interface plants ILife's odd Step(int speed) — 2speed ticks — for later.

Path two: an n-quad is a 2ⁿ-square as an immutable quadtree whose leaves are doubletons — exactly two leaf objects, Quad.Dead and Quad.Alive. "This is bonkers!" (16 bits of grid as seven heap objects), but there are only 2 zero-quads, 16 one-quads, 65,536 two-quads — so memoize the constructor: Make(nw, ne, se, sw) deduplicates through a Memoizer keyed on the tuple, and identical subtrees become the identical reference. MaxLevel = 60 ("a 60-quad ought to be enough for anyone" — it would have more mass than the Sun); the empty 60-quad is 2¹²⁰ cells in 61 small objects. Memory becomes a function of irregularity, not grid size. Rico Mariani supplies the aphorism: "A cache with a bad policy is another name for a memory leak."

HashLife's engine exploits a fact: any n-quad for n>1 determines its center (n−1)-quad some ticks ahead. Base case — a 2-quad determines exactly its center 1-quad one tick ahead. Two bugs are fixed on the way. The shrinking grid: stepping yields an (n−1)-quad, so live cells nearing the edge trigger Embiggen() — dead space "is so cheap as to be practically free." The exponential worry: nine recursions per level looks like a "horrifying" O(9n−2) — but Step is pure, therefore memoizable, and measurements over 5,000 ticks show a power-law cache: 20 entries absorb 40% of all calls, a few hundred reach 50%, while 97% of entries are hit fewer than 20 times and half never again. The cold tail wastes memory — hence a self-tuning reset: every 512 calls, if caches exceed maxCache (initially 200,000), clear them, then double maxCache.

Then the missed trick that unlocks everything (figure 4.11 asks you to spot it): after assembling four stepped 2-quads, don't take their Center() — call Step() on them. The ladder becomes: a 2-quad gives 1 tick, a 3-quad 2, a 4-quad 4 — an n-quad yields its center (n−1)-quad 2n−2 ticks ahead via just 13 memoized recursions per level. That is why Step(speed) is logarithmic: for 1,024 ticks, embiggen to a 12-quad.

The honest ledger: HashLife is slow during the initial chaos, then approaches O(1) time per generation regardless of grid size, with memory proportional to variation — "trillions of generations in seconds." The techniques (dedup via memoized constructors, cache tuning) transferred straight to Lippert's day job — starting with a Scrabble dictionary.

Takeaways

  • Two paths to performance: tune hot spots (1,200 ticks/s → 10× → 200×, all O(n)) or change the frame.
  • Memoize pure constructors and identical structure becomes the identical reference — memory ∝ irregularity.
  • HashLife ladder: 2-quad → 1 tick; n-quad → center 2n−2 ticks ahead in 13 recursions; Step(speed) is logarithmic.
  • Cache measurement is part of the algorithm: power-law hit rates justify the self-tuning maxCache reset.

CHAPTER 5

What's up with you, Directed Acyclic Word Graph?

Sequel to the 1996 interview: the second interviewer asked something much better — given the rack NISATEV, find the Scrabble bingos: NAIVEST, NATIVES, VAINEST. Lippert solved it, then fumbled the follow-up: "Do you know what a dog is?" He meant DAWG — Directed Acyclic Word Graph. "That was my second no-hire of the day." Stakes are real: the C# IDE team had a 30-millisecond IntelliSense budget.

The ADT is IWords: Contains(word) and StartsWith(prefix). Hash sets are a nonsolution — O(m) Contains, but "essentially useless" for prefixes, because well-designed hashes deliberately scatter similar words; Lippert once "ruined the performance of an early version of Microsoft.com" with a hash that clustered them. A sorted list is "…fine?" — binary search gives O(m log n) for both, via the i = ~i complement trick. The real cost is memory: ENABLE's 172,820 words cost ≈8 MB as a List<string>, and every GC has 172,820 objects to trace.

A trie deduplicates prefixes: search drops to O(m) — "called tries because they're for retrieving words. Get it? It's a silly joke." But the hidden failure is suffixes: on ENABLE the trie has 387,881 nodes, and 111,507 words are prefixes of nothing, each with its own logically identical end-leaf — a megabyte of redundancy. "We're not saving any memory" over the sorted list.

The reframe: a trie is a finite state automaton — nodes are states, edge labels inputs, double circles success states; the accepted set is the machine's language. Minimize the automaton and you get the DAWG (his term; the synonym is DAFSA).

But build-then-minimize is useless when the trie doesn't fit in memory, so the Daciuk–Watson algorithm (1998) builds an almost-minimal graph one word at a time, maintaining the invariant: the graph is minimal for every word except the nodes of the last word added. Ordinal-sorted input required (mind the German ß/"ss" ordering trap). The subtlety is delicious: adding fire must not prematurely merge node 9 with node 5 — the next word makes them inequivalent, and merging early would silently add "carese" to the language. Equivalence is structural (same IsEnd, same edge count, same labels, reference-identical targets), enforced by a HashSet of canonical nodes — which may only contain never-again-mutated nodes, the chapter's hash-set safety rule finally paying off.

The payoff on ENABLE: 54,167 nodes vs the trie's 387,881 — 86% fewer (only 14% as many), 122,975 edges, and exactly one zero-edge node. Retro-engineering flourish: game developers of the 640 KB era flattened the DAWG into one byte array — a 4-byte header per node (one IsEnd bit plus one adjacency bit per alphabet letter), one 3-byte offset per edge — packing ENABLE into 585,593 bytes. "A wonderful combination of elegance, efficiency, and searchability even in environments that are extremely short on memory." One query layer, WordGraph, serves trie and DAWG unchanged: asymptotics O(m) search, O(mn) build.

⚠ Erratum watch. As printed, the card’s last-edge-label walk under-merges the book’s own nine-word example (11 nodes vs figure 5.13’s 10); walking the previous word’s actual suffix reproduces the figure. The Python materialization’s fix_up_last_word already does so (it takes the last word and prefix length), so its output matches figure 5.13.

Takeaways

  • Ladder: hash set (no prefixes) → sorted list O(m log n) → trie O(m) → DAWG, same O(m) on 86% fewer nodes.
  • Tries are FSAs; DAWGs are their minimized form — and the Daciuk invariant ("minimal except the last word") builds minimal directly.
  • Premature merging is a correctness bug, not an optimization: it would have added "carese" to English.

CHAPTER 6

Combinatorial algorithms

The BCL ships Aggregate, Where, Join — "but doesn't come with algorithms to generate all the permutations or combinations of a sequence." Lippert has always written his own (usually for test-case generation) and is, ironically, grateful: "simple, elegant, timeless, classic algorithms that I learned a lot from." The chapter's unifying insight: Cartesian products, permutations, and combinations all output sequences of sequences, so asking "what is the p-th one?" reveals nonstandard ways to decompose integers — decimal digits, then the factorial base, then the combinatorial base.

Cartesian product. Nested foreach "emphasizes the mechanism, not the meaning"; the general version over arbitrarily many sequences starts from the signature IEnumerable<IEnumerable<T>>, seeds with the single empty deque, and folds each input sequence in with a query expression — building lazily on chapter 3's O(1) PushRight, O(n) to construct, sorted inputs giving lexicographic output. (Zero sequences? One empty sequence.)

Permutations. There are n! of them — "worse than exponential" — so the chapter both enumerates and ranks/unranks. Narayana Pandita's algorithm (about 700 years old) mutates an array to the next lexicographic permutation, handling duplicates for free (ABBEY's 60 orderings), and inherits chapter 3's amortization logic: on average 3 comparisons and 1.5 swaps per step, amortized O(1). Unranking lexicographically peels a factorial base — 9 = 1·3!+1·2!+1·1!+0·0!, written 1110; 19 is 3010 — with BigInteger arithmetic whose honest cost is O(n²) from RemoveAt, fixable to O(n log n) with a deque split. The punchline: Fisher–Yates shuffle digits are factorial-base digits under a different ordering — same permutations, cheaper unranking, non-lexicographic order. Change ringing (English church bells, 17th century) demands successive permutations differ by one adjacent swap, cyclically; the recursive table solution is O(n²) lazily, and Even's algorithm (Steinhaus–Johnson–Trotter; Shimon Even, 1973) does O(n) per permutation with "mobile" numbers — never yielding the array it keeps mutating (copy before every yield).

Combinations (order-preserving k-subsequences — "what happens when we skip things"): the next-combination mutation, the immutable deque version, and the counting identities — Choose(n,k) = nCk = nC(n−k), Pascal's recurrence, 20C10 = 184,756. Beware a *= b/c: integer division rounds, so 66×13/3 ≠ 66×(13/3); write result = result * (n - k + i) / i. Unranking recurses on the boundary (n−1)Ck, and the inverse — index(0245) = (0C1)+(2C2)+(4C3)+(5C4) = 10 — needs no n at all: every p < nCk has a unique representation p = Σ xᵢC(i+1), the combinatorial base (formally the Macaulay representation; D.H. Lehmer's ranking application). The integers, it turns out, "contain structures you may not have noticed previously."

Takeaways

  • Enumeration orders mirror number systems: decimal → factorial base (Fisher–Yates = its digits) → combinatorial/Macaulay base.
  • Pandita: in-place, duplicate-friendly, amortized O(1) (3 comparisons, 1.5 swaps); Even's/SJT: one adjacent swap per step at O(n) each.
  • Iterator hygiene: yield copies of anything the generator keeps mutating; and integer division inside *= is a rounding bug.
  • Ranking/unranking is the practical payoff — random combination = random p, then unrank.

INTERLUDE · CHAPTER 7

First abstract nonsense interlude: Category theory

"What could be better than messing around with generalized abstract nonsense?" Category theorists self-describe that way, and Lippert's reasons for the detour: composition is software's fundamental strategy (category theory is "the study of composable operations"), it changed how he thinks about programming and language design, and fun. A category is just objects — anything at all — plus morphisms, arrows obeying two rules: reflexive (every object has its identity arrow) and transitive (A→B and B→C gives A→C). A morphism means "you can get from here to there," and the stuff underneath doesn't matter.

Two deliberately parallel examples: objects {0,1,2} with an arrow x→y whenever y ≥ x (three objects, six morphisms — a posetal category); and objects Eric, Bruce, Bob, Ellroy with arrows "is an ancestor of or identical to" (four objects, ten morphisms). Its bottom three-quarters has the same shape despite completely different stuff. That's the setup for functors: a plain function like F(int) => family[i] maps objects across categories (dashed arrows — explicitly not morphisms), but a function that always preserves morphisms is a covariant functor; if source and target category are the same, a covariant endofunctor.

Now the category of types: objects Giraffe, Tiger, Animal, Object; morphisms are assignment compatibility — again posetal, Giraffe and Tiger incomparable. The chapter-2 callback lands: is a sequence of giraffes a sequence of animals? Give IE<T> only output positions, declare IE<out T>, and the map T ↦ IE<T> preserves every arrow. Totality makes it an endofunctor: IE<IE<Giraffe>>, IE<IE<IE<Giraffe>>>… the infinite tower of constructed types is part of the category too. "That is why we call IE<T> a covariant generic type. Language designers took this term straight from category theory." Fun fact: that infinite category is a semilattice — "what's the most specific type both expressions can be assigned to?" is a greatest-lower-bound query, and semantic analyzers exploit lattices. It is also, in the field's sense of the word, "small": it's "only" infinite.

Contravariance completes the picture: "an animal-comparer is also a giraffe-comparer… seems to be backward" — yet it's correct, because a device comparing any two animals can compare two giraffes. With IC<in T> (T only in input positions), the map reverses arrow direction: a contravariant functor, and in IC<IC<T>> the arrows point the normal way again — reversed twice. The kinesthetic image: two points moving along morphisms — same direction, covariant; opposite, contravariant.

Project status: nothing added to Fabulous.Collections — this interlude pays off ch2's IImStack<out T> in theory instead. interface IE<out T> / interface IC<in T> are the entire "code."

Takeaways

  • Category = objects + reflexive, transitive arrows; posetal categories cover both ≥ and type assignment.
  • Functor = morphism-preserving map; totality over the infinite type tower is what upgrades it to endofunctor.
  • out T / in T are category theory with the serial numbers visible; IC<IC<T>> re-reverses.
Part 2 · Chapters 8–11

Searching, solving, inferring

The odd algorithms of Lippert's developer-tools career: backtracking search, greedy formatting, and the unification machinery behind code analysis — plus a monad interlude.

CHAPTER 8

Coloring graphs with backtracking search

Assign colors to nodes so adjacent nodes never share one — map regions, Sudoku cells, compiler registers. Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, and Paraguay mutually border, so they form a clique and need four distinct colors; the four-color theorem (proved only in the late 20th century) says four always suffice, though real maps use more: counting the ocean as blue forces one of Bolivia/Paraguay to be blue too, which "looks strange," and legally France is adjacent to Brazil via French Guiana.

The substrate is ImMulti<K,V>, a thin wrapper over ImmutableDictionary<K, ImmutableHashSet<V>> (no such type ships in .NET; all ops O(1)), wrapped again in ImGraph<N> — a miniature design lesson: good types enforce invariants (the raw multidictionary happily leaves adjacency asymmetric and Bolivia adjacent to a non-node — "this is a mess"), speak in jargon of nodes and edges rather than dictionaries, and hide the implementation. AddEdge writes both directions; AddClique is O(n²).

The simple recursive algorithm peels a node of degree < color-count to color last (a degree-d node colored last always has a free color if d < c), recurses, then picks any unused color. It colors South America in four colors, running between O(n+e) and O(n²+e). Its fatal limitation: every Sudoku cell has degree 20 against only 9 colors — "it can't even get started." (81 cells = nodes; rows, columns, and 3×3 boxes are 27 nine-cliques.)

Cue the digression: graph coloring is NP-complete — yes/no, polynomially verifiable, no known polynomial algorithm, no impossibility proof, and one fast algorithm would give them all. "I believe that there's no such algorithm, but I could be wrong." Backtracking is therefore allowed to be exponential; the job is to shrink the guess space first. Guessing itself is cheap because the graph is immutable: a guess is a new persistent value, and undo is free. The engine has three parts: an Attempt (nodes → remaining colors; one value each = solved; any empty = broken), a Reducer (IReducer<K,V>) that propagates constraints without guessing — every single-color node eliminates its color from all neighbors, iterated to a fixpoint — and a generic Backtracker whose Solve is seven lines with nothing graph-specific in them.

Chapter 6 echoes loudly: two disconnected islands with four colors yield 16 solutions — literally the Cartesian product — and backtracking "essentially enumerates the Cartesian product of possible solutions" via composed SelectManys, filtering broken attempts early. (That pattern is chapter 11's monad.) The same machinery schedules airport gates (160 "colors"), builds school timetables, and does register allocation: variables are nodes, overlapping lifetimes are edges, registers are colors, and a failed coloring means spilling the cheapest variable to memory. Sudoku hobbyists call guess-and-backtrack bifurcation and give it "a bad reputation" — their dozens of deductions could be encoded into the reducer, but Lippert deliberately stops.

Takeaways

  • Attempt / Reducer / Backtracker: constraint propagation to a fixpoint, then guessing — the Backtracker is fully problem-agnostic.
  • Persistent structures make "go back and make a different guess" free; that's why immutability suits search.
  • Coloring is NP-complete — so reduce aggressively and accept exponential worst cases knowingly.
  • Search = exploring a solution space, with reduction pruning regions that can't contain a solution.

CHAPTER 9

Greedy iterative pretty printing

Every team Lippert has worked on has two rules: everyone runs the same automatic formatter before check-in, and never reformat existing files otherwise. This chapter builds the formatter's core. The problem: parse tree back to pleasant text, with three goals in strict priority — (1) no line over the width limit (80 or 100 chars) unless necessary; (2) indentation that helps the reader; (3) as few line breaks as possible. Simplifications to keep the algorithm visible: no comments, no tabs, fixed 4-space indent, expressions only.

It's a greedy algorithm: solve each subproblem selfishly and combine. Greedy can be globally wrong — the change-making example: 73¢ optimally needs 7 US coins and greedy finds it, but take away the nickels and 41¢ defeats greedy: 8 coins (quarter, dime, six pennies) where 4 dimes + 1 penny gives 5. Backtracking (chapter 8) finds the true optimum but is expensive; an IDE must reformat huge files while being edited, so a fast acceptable answer beats a slow optimal one. Lineage: Oppen (1980) → Wadler's "A Prettier Printer" (1998) → Lindig's "Strictly Pretty" (2000), simplified here; Lippert also strongly recommends Hughes' 1995 pretty-printing library paper — the Hughes-list Hughes — "as much a tutorial on problem-solving and principled library design as it is about pretty printing."

Architecture: phase 1 turns a parse tree into a Doc — an immutable DAG of layout desires (TextDoc, OptBreakDoc, GroupDoc, IndentDoc, ConcatDoc) — and phase 2 renders it, deliberately taught doc-first because the transformation only makes sense once formatting semantics are understood. Groups decide all their optional breaks all-or-nothing by asking Fits(width − used). The docs run deep: 17 levels for 21 characters of source, and depth grows with file size — so both Fits and Pretty shun recursion and use explicit heap-allocated Stack<T>s of pending work, (bool fits, int indent, Doc) per item, constant call-stack space. The input is wrapped in a fresh outer group so every break has an enclosing group. Honest imperfection: at width 15 the sample overflows by one character — never breaking before the closing paren made it unavoidable. "It's not perfect, but by definition, good enough is good enough."

Phase 1 refuses the obvious design — a virtual ToDoc() on every parse-tree class — with three Conway's-Law arguments: the editor team may not own the compiler team's tree; multiple pretty printers would mean AliceToDoc, BobToDoc…; and formatting is one of many cross-cutting passes (coloring, linting, folding) that would bloat the hierarchy. Instead, the visitor pattern — which Lippert would rename double dispatch: the invoked method depends on two runtime types, via Accept then Visit. The Accept boilerplate was so tedious in the C# compiler that he scripted its generation ("the only risk is excessive boredom"). The visitor encodes formatting policy as data: operators grouped with left operands, breaks after open-parens and commas inside one all-or-nothing group, optional break before the dot. Closing thesis, and his most important thing about software design: "you can create a library that makes concise programs that encode the concepts of a specific domain."

Takeaways

  • Three prioritized goals — width, indentation, fewest breaks — and greedy fits-as-much-as-possible semantics per group.
  • Explicit stacks, not recursion: docs get deep, call stacks are fixed-size.
  • Visitor = double dispatch across team boundaries; keep cross-cutting passes out of the parse-tree hierarchy.
  • "Good enough is good enough" — the greedy tradeoff justified by the nickelless till.

CHAPTER 10

Unification and anti-unification

Unification is "an intimidating jargon word for a straightforward concept": given two things with holes, find stuff for the holes that makes them equal, like A²+6 = 5×A (A is 2 or 3). Here the things are data structures: chapter 2's stacks with holes X and Y, then binary terms — Hole, Constant, or Symbol(name, left, right), compared structurally. A substitution is a mutable dictionary from holes to terms; a hole with an entry is bound, else free. Unification goes general→specific; anti-unification runs specific→general, keeping common structure and hole-ifying differences. The chapter shows two wrong algorithms on purpose.

First attempt: bind holes, recurse on same-name symbols. Counterexample: X demanded as both 2 and a stack containing X — the algorithm overwrites the binding and recurses until the stack explodes. Diagnosis: an occurs check is needed — no hole may be substituted by a term containing itself. Second attempt adds it and still fails: ImStack(Y, Y) is legal, but binding X→Y then Y→a stack containing X cycles forever — holes can alias holes. A bound hole rebound to two values must have its candidates unified with each other — which only happens if you chase chains first.

The fix is Robinson's 1965 algorithm, "enormously influential in the study of automated logic": look up bound holes first (chase the chain), succeed on structural equality, bind free holes only after the occurs check, recurse on same-name symbols, else fail. Performance is the scandal: unify four holes arranged as the Blah towers and the substituted result allocates O(2ⁿ) objects (4 holes → 16 nodes; 7 → 128), because substitution rebuilds the world per occurrence. The HashLife echo: memoize term factories so structural equality becomes reference equality and duplicates deduplicate — the exponential graph becomes linear. Optimized, worst case O(n³); linear algorithms exist but are unused. "In practice, we almost always use Robinson's algorithm despite its terrible worst case" — use the simplest algorithm with acceptable results, the chapter-9 principle again.

Two applications. Type inference is unification: generic parameters are "essentially free holes" (T and U here; the return is hole V), so Frob<A,B>(A a, Func<A,B> f) called with 1.5 and x => [x] unifies and yields T→double, U→List<double>, V→List<List<double>>. Logic programming: facts plus the rule "likes(X,Y) and likes(Z,Y) → compatible(X,Z)" — the goal compatible(Bob, Q) unifies, spawns subgoals, and backtracking through Y's two values yields Q ∈ {Alice, Bob, Carol}: unification + chapter 8's backtracking = Prolog (1972), the fact-producing early AI "rather than using statistical likelihood to produce plausible hallucinations and plagiarized slop."

Anti-unification (Reynolds and Plotkin, late 1960s) computes the most specific generalization: Mult(Add(1,2), Div(Add(1,2), 5)) and Mult(6, Div(6,5)) share two similarities, so the answer is Mult(A, Div(A, 5)) with sub1: A→Add(1,2), sub2: A→6 — not the lossier Mult(X, Div(Y, Z)). Equal terms recurse; same-name symbols recurse; an existing hole with matching (sub1, sub2) entries is reused — that preserves the shared left operand; otherwise a fresh hole. O(n²) naive — the reuse-scan "is essentially doing the job of a memoizer, badly" — O(n) with memoized factories and a memoized AU. At Facebook, Lippert's tools team anti-unified thousands of null-dereference fixes into a dozen ranked patterns (before: B.A(); after: if (B != null) B.A(); and friends), then unified new buggy code against the pattern-befores: "the tool usually generated a plausible fix."

Takeaways

  • Two deliberate failures motivate two rules — occurs check, look-up-bound-holes-first; Robinson's exponential worst case is tamed to linear by memoized factories (HashLife's dedup again).
  • Type inference = term unification; unification + backtracking = Prolog.
  • Anti-unification = most specific generalization; at scale it learns bug-fix patterns and proposes them back.

INTERLUDE · CHAPTER 11

Second abstract nonsense interlude: Monads

"In every programming language enthusiast's life, there comes a time when they try to explain monads to anyone who will listen, and I'm no exception." Through category-theory glasses, a monad is an endofunctor on the category of types obeying the monad laws; through OOP glasses it's "a design pattern for powerful, composable generic types" — a generic type that adds a capability while preserving the workflow. The roster, each phrased as "adds the ability to…": Nullable<T> (be null), Func<T> (compute on demand), Lazy<T> (= Func plus caching), Task<T> (compute asynchronously), IObservable<T> (produce when something happens), IEnumerable<T> (produce many values, one at a time). Central claim: any workflow over integers can be transformed into one over nullable, lazy, asynchronous, or sequenced integers — that transformation is the point.

The laboratory is one trivial function, DivTwo, lifted by hand into each monad. The liftings differ, and the differences are the meaning: nullable propagates null (unwrap, compute, rewrap — the rewrap is Unit); Lazy defers everything into a lambda; the Task version must await — synchronous unwrap-and-rewrap "doesn't preserve the capability of the monad"; sequences foreach and yield. Where and how unwrapping happens is the monad's semantics.

Two operations carry everything. Unit: T → M<T> (wrapping must always be possible). Bind: (M<T>, Func<T, M<R>>) → M<R>. Bind exists because Map on a function that already returns M<R> produces the nesting pathology — Lazy<Lazy<double>>, Nullable<Nullable<R>>, "something seems amiss" — and Bind flattens. Everything else is derivable: Map(m, f) = Bind(m, t => Unit(f(t))) and Join(mmt) = Bind(mmt, x => x). "Once again, we're seeing why category theory is called 'generalized abstract nonsense.'"

The payoff is that LINQ is the sequence monad in disguise: Select is Map (C# chose SQL-flavored names for database programmers; Python and Java say map), SelectMany is Bind (flatMap). Even Where derives from Unit and an additive identity: items.SelectMany(t => predicate(t) ? [t] : []) — "absurdly inefficient because it allocates so many tiny sequences, but it works." That makes sequences an additive monad: values add (concatenation), the empty sequence is MZero, and Bind on MZero yields MZero. Chapter 6's Cartesian product was SelectMany as "multiplication of sequences" — and multiplying by zero gives zero: Bind is a bit like a multiplication of monads. Part 3 will need the additive Where for "a surprising application."

Takeaways

  • A monad adds a capability while preserving the workflow; unwrap/wrap placement defines its semantics (async must await).
  • Unit + Bind are primitives; Map and Join are theorems; the M<M<R>> pathology is Bind's reason to exist.
  • Select = Map, SelectMany = Bind, Where = Bind against Unit/MZero: LINQ is an additive monad.
Part 3 · Chapters 12–16

Probabilities

A first-class abstraction for randomness, Bayes' theorem as composable code, and the Metropolis algorithm — ending in principled decisions under uncertainty.

CHAPTER 12

A better abstraction for randomness

Lippert skipped his one required statistics course ("the jargon is confusing") and paid for it implementing data-science tools. The goal: give randomness what LINQ gave sequences — a first-class abstraction so code "reads like what it does." Two philosophies frame it. Frequentist: probability is the long-run fraction of repeated trials — useless for one-off events. Bayesian: probability is degree of confidence, operationalized as a fair price — 70% confidence justifies charging $70 for a $100 bet. The 10¹⁴th digit of pi is already even or odd: a frequentist says 0% or 100%, a Bayesian says 50% absent evidence. The book's policy: frequentist sampling to check the work, Bayesian attitude for the math.

The interfaces embody a design decision: IDistribution<T> with Sample(), and IDiscreteDistribution<T> adding Support() and Weight(t) — probabilities as positive integer weights (P(t) = weight/total), because double probabilities may not sum to exactly 1.0, and rounding later breaks the alias method. System.Random is a one-use tool for the discrete uniform — and it's pseudorandom: attackers can deduce past and future outputs, so use RandomNumberGenerator wherever money or keys are involved. DiscreteUniform, Singleton (the double-headed coin), and Bernoulli follow the factory-plus-private-constructor pattern; Bernoulli reduces 30:70 to 3:7 via Euclid's GCD — small weights matter soon. A verification culture runs throughout: Histogram() over 100,000 samples shows the 30/70 coin landing 30,182/69,818.

The workhorse is Projected<T,R>: map a distribution's support through a function, regroup and sum the weights, GCD-reduce, collapse to a Singleton. A colored die is just the fair die projected — weights green:1, blue:3, red:2. That construction is the categorical distribution: arbitrary finite support, arbitrary weights — "the most general finite discrete distribution." The rest of the chapter is a tournament of four samplers for it:

The four categorical samplers: space / construction / per-sample cost.
AlgorithmSpaceConstructionSample
1 · big list (repeat each category by weight)O(W)O(W)O(1)
2 · ladder (cumulative rungs; binary-search sketch)O(n)O(n)O(n), O(log n) searchable
3 · rejection (dartboard; weights [1,1,1,40] starve it)O(n)O(n)unbounded worst case
4 · alias methodO(n)O(n)O(1), never rejects

The alias method is the winner: spread each category's "area" across an n×W board by moving squares from too-wide rows into too-narrow ones (≤n iterations) until every row holds exactly W squares — and at most two distinct values. Each row becomes a Singleton or a projected Bernoulli; sampling is two O(1) samples (pick a row uniformly, then its row distribution), never a rejection, and zero-weight categories are harmless. Finally, combinators: ToCategorical and Filter — re-roll-by-construction, the exact tool chapter 13 will need. And one deferred question — why distributions don't just inherit IEnumerable<T> — is answered in chapter 14.

Takeaways

  • Integer weights trade rounding safety for GCD bookkeeping — a bet that pays off in chapter 13.
  • Projected over a uniform gives the categorical distribution; the alias method samples it in O(1) with two draws, no rejection.
  • Rejection sampling is educational and unbounded; its redemption arrives in chapter 15.
  • Project and Filter make distributions composable — the LINQ analogy made real.

CHAPTER 13

Conditional probability with Bayes' theorem

Chapter 12 built the parts; this chapter "combines those basic parts to unlock their true power" — Bayes' theorem computes posteriors: updating previous opinions on new evidence. Thomas Bayes, an 18th-century British statistician, "didn't live to see his work on probability theory published"; his theorem lets us "reason backward in time." The running example is a 10,000-person survey (do you have a cold? did you sneeze in the past 24 hours?), summarized in a marginal table — named for the totals on its margins:

Table 13.1 — the cold/sneeze survey as a marginal table.
Cold: YESCold: NOTotal
Sneezed: YES8602701,130
Sneezed: NO1408,7308,870
Total1,0009,00010,000

From it, the whole taxonomy: prior P(C) = 10%; conditional P(S|C) = 86%; joint P(C&S) = 8.6%; P(S) = 11.3%; and the posterior P(C|S) = 860/1,130 = 76.1%. (Notation warning, boxed in the book: the bar in P(S|C) means if, not or — "somewhat unfortunate.") Two identities fall out — P(C)×P(S|C) = P(C&S) and P(S)×P(C|S) = P(C&S) — and equating them is Bayes' theorem. The update is dramatic: a random person is 10% likely to have a cold; learning they sneezed moves belief to 76.1% — "an enormous update." The modeling insight: colds cause sneezing, so the likelihood function is a time-invariant fact about the world, independent of the seasonal prior.

In code, each term of the theorem has an exact analogue: the prior is an IDiscreteDistribution<A> object; the likelihood is Func<A, IDiscreteDistribution<B>>; the joint is ToJoint; the posterior is just Filter the joint to the observed evidence, then Project back to the cause. "That's the essence of diagnosis: observe effects and reason backwards to causes." The one engineering hurdle is integer weights: prior 1-of-10 times likelihood 43-of-50 is fractional, so ToJoint scales by the LCM of all conditional total weights (built from chapter 12's GCD) so every joint weight stays an integer.

The flagship: Frob Syndrome, a fictitious condition striking 1 in 30,000, with a cheap 99.5%-accurate test. A positive result — and the posterior is 0.7% (weights No:29,999, Yes:199). "Be immediately suspicious of any reasoning that gives a posterior without mentioning the prior." Then Part 3's opening question pays off: 999 normal coins and 1 double-headed coin; ten heads in a row; posterior weights Normal:999, DoubleHeaded:1024 — barely better than even odds, because P(10 heads|normal) = 1/1024 almost exactly matches the 1/1000 prior odds. Independence gets a fun special case: Dungeons & Dragons roll-with-advantage (d20 twice, keep higher) gives weights n:(2n−1) — a 20 is 39× likelier than a 1. The chapter ends by introducing JointProject and promising an "astonishing" fact about it: chapter 14 reveals it as Bind.

Takeaways

  • Every term of Bayes' theorem has a code analogue: prior = object, likelihood = function, joint = ToJoint, posterior = Filter+Project.
  • A positive result on a 99.5% test for a 1-in-30,000 condition still means ~0.7% — priors are not optional.
  • 999:1024 after ten heads: evidence barely shifts belief when likelihood and prior odds align.
  • LCM arithmetic keeps the integer-weight promise through joint distributions.

INTERLUDE · CHAPTER 14

Third abstract nonsense interlude: The probability monad

The promised "astonishing fact": the distribution type is already a monad. The capability is chapter 12's (IDiscreteDistribution<T> conforms to a PMF); the Unit is Singleton<T>; and the missing Bind is chapter 13's JointProject in disguise — treat the monadic value as a prior, the function as a likelihood, build the joint, and project the second element. Bind's output even explains a word: binding SneezedGivenCold to the 10% prior yields No:887, Yes:113 — read straight off the right margin of the joint table. "That's why we call this distribution marginal."

From Unit and Bind, chapter 11's derivations come free: Map is exactly Project, and Join flattens a distribution of distributions by binding the identity — flip a fair coin, then roll d6 on tails and d10 on heads, and Join gives one unfair ten-sider (weights 8,8,8,8,8,8,3,3,3,3), so "the generic types never have to get nested too deeply." The probability monad is even additive: two distributions add by merging supports and weights (pour two urns of marbles together), MZero is Empty<T> — "everything is impossible" — and the generic Where falls out as Bind against Unit/MZero. Lippert admits it's "simply a less efficient, less readable version of the Filter function we developed in chapter 12": the point is theoretical.

Then the honest critique. Good news: statistical jargon on statistical objects; O(n) construction and O(1) sampling for any finite discrete distribution. Bad news: integer weights, which enabled the alias method, make joint distributions hard (chapter 15 switches to non-normalized fractional weights); joints cost O(mn) time and space — "we've chosen to optimize the asymptotic cost of sampling by spending potentially a lot on computing joint distributions"; and infinite discrete supports are out of reach — the Poisson distribution (emails per year, uranium decays per minute) can't be represented. Verdict: "it works well for categorical distributions with small supports, and that's something. But it's fair to say that this is a very small corner of the whole space of statistical problems." The closing arc: sampling random sequences and estimating continuous posteriors are "closely related in a surprising way" — chapters 15–16 deliver.

Takeaways

  • Singleton = Unit; ToJoint + Project(Item2) = Bind (the marginal); Project = Map; Bind(id) = Join — the monad assembled from parts already built.
  • Empty<T> is MZero; distributions form an additive monad, with Where as a theorem rather than a tool.
  • Limits, stated honestly: O(mn) joints, integer-weight friction, no Poisson — "a very small corner."

CHAPTER 15

Sampling continuous distributions

The last two chapters redo part 3 for continuous distributions — random real numbers — motivated not just by physical quantities like manufacturing tolerances but by the fact that "probabilities themselves are real numbers": the belief "this new account is ~90% a bot" is a real-valued quantity to update with evidence. A PDF maps a real to a non-negative real with finite area; the running example is the beta-ish P(x) = x0.5(1−x)1.5 on [0,1]. Sampling "is like throwing a dart uniformly at the shaded area — the x coordinate of the point is the sample," so P(below 0.5) is just sub-area over total area: ≈0.06/0.2 ≈ 32%. A PDF with total area exactly 1 is normalized, but "you'll often deal with non-normalized PDFs in practice" — the theme chapter 16's miracle depends on. New interfaces encode the break with chapter 12: supports can't be enumerated and weights are positive reals, so IWeightedDistribution<T> (with Weight(x)) and IContinuousDistribution replace Support/Weight-by-integers.

Method 1 is the continuous uniform (on [0,1], the standard distribution). Method 1½ is the normal distribution — the widget machine aiming at 60.0 mm ± 0.1 mm, tails "extremely thin" past four standard deviations — sampled by the Box–Muller transform: pick a random radius and a random angle in polar coordinates and the x coordinate is normally distributed; rescale and shift for any mean and standard deviation. Method 2 is the inverse transform, the continuous analogue of chapter 12's ladder: normalize the PDF, integrate to the CDF (P(sample ≤ x); a monotone climb from 0 to 1 — "almost all CDFs have a stretched S shape, called a sigmoid"), invert it to the quantile function, and feed standard-uniform samples in. The showcase is the Cauchy distribution — bell-shaped with much fatter tails than the normal — which needs just three short lambdas: PDF 1/(π(1+x²)), CDF atan(x)/π + 0.5, quantile tan(π(p−0.5)).

Method 3 is rejection sampling, promoted from chapter 12's categorical dartboard: it needs exactly three things — the (possibly non-normalized) target PDF, a helper distribution we can already sample whose support covers the target's, and a scale factor making scaled-helper ≥ target everywhere. The two-hump test case — Exp(−x·x) + Exp((1.0−x)(x−1.0)·10.0), pretending we don't know it's two normals — needs the standard normal scaled by a hand-tuned 2.5. A benign sub-application is Clamp(0.0, 1.0): cut the absurd tails off a Normal(0.5, 0.2) model of "probability of breakdown" — and that clamped normal is precisely chapter 16's prior. But two failures disqualify rejection as the general tool: rejections "can be arbitrarily large" (in the two-hump case the reject area ≈ the accept area), and "there's no general way to automate figuring out which helper distribution and scale factor work" — Lippert hand-tuned 2.5 in a spreadsheet. "We'd like to be able to sample automatically from any distribution."

Takeaways

  • Four methods, in order of automation: special-purpose (uniform, Box–Muller), inverse transform (needs a quantile), rejection (needs helper + scale), Metropolis (chapter 16).
  • Non-normalized PDFs are a feature: nothing here divides by total area.
  • Rejection's two failure modes — unbounded rejections and unautomatable helper choice — are exactly what Metropolis fixes.
  • Clamped Normal(0.5, 0.2) is the canonical benign rejection — and the finale's prior.

CHAPTER 16

Markov processes and the Metropolis algorithm

The finale announces a surprise identity: "the Markov process — which language models use to generate random text — is also the basis of the Metropolis algorithm for sampling from continuous posterior distributions." A Markov process starts in a random initial state, then repeatedly transitions to a new state chosen based only on the current one; a sample is a sequence of states. In code, Markov<T> takes an initial IDistribution<T> and a transition Func<T, IDistribution<T>> — which is exactly chapter 13's likelihood-function shape, and returning chapter 14's Empty<T> terminates the sequence. The gambler's ruin demo (±1 chip, absorbed at 0 and 10) shows sequence lengths peaking near 8–9 flips — with one 287-flip outlier in 100,000. Simulators for Brownian motion, DNA mutation, work queues: "Markov processes are everywhere!"

Then the Shakespeare generator: split the complete works into sentences, make the initial distribution over first words and the transition over following words, and "in a few dozen lines of code (plus a couple hundred thousand lines of Shakespeare), we've built a very small language model." The output is "recognizably Shakespearean, but of course it doesn't make sense." The LLM ladder is precise: 8,254 distinct words follow "the," but over 5,000 of them appear after it exactly once ("the puddle"), so the raw process is ~18× likelier than it should be to pick an exotic follower; bigger states (word pairs, triples) sharpen context. LLMs take the state to be the whole session, making generation potentially quadratic in document length; pirated copyrighted corpora, bias (doctor/nurse associations), and armies of low-paid training contractors complete the comparison. The sharpest observation is philosophical: small and large models share "the location of intention" — the desire to fool the reader "belongs to the authors of the models, not to the random text-generation algorithm."

Back to Bayes. For continuous quantities the theorem works unchanged, except P(evidence) is unknown — but it's a constant for fixed evidence, and dividing a PDF by a constant "changes only the total area, not the relative weight of any member of the support." So the posterior PDF is simply a => prior.Weight(a) * likelihood(a).Weight(evidence) — provided something can sample a non-normalized PDF. Rejection sampling can't (it must know the posterior's shape, "which is what we're trying to determine in the first place"). Metropolis (Nicolas Metropolis, 1950s) can, in five steps: sample the initial distribution; propose from a distribution centered on the current sample; compute the quotient target(proposed)/target(current); accept iff a standard-uniform ≤ the quotient; else keep the current sample. Only the quotient matters, so normalization cancels — and each sample costs constant work, no loops. Tuning: the initial distribution must land in the support (the prior is perfect for posteriors); the proposal must be unbiased; Normal(current, 1.0) is "a sweet spot."

The deepest joke: Metropolis is a Markov process — the implementation literally reuses Markov<double> with a Flip transition, closing the chapter's identity. The finale assembles the whole book: prior = chapter 15's Normal.Distribution(0.5, 0.2).Clamp(0.0, 1.0); likelihood = a new binomial over heads in 10 flips, whose weight uses chapter 6's Choose; observe 9 heads in 10 and the posterior histogram's mass moves hard toward 0.9 fairness — "very unlikely that the coin is 50% (or less) fair." The same pipeline models hostile-botnet vs human accounts (spam, scams, misinformation, election interference as evidence). And the closing moral of the book's final chapter: "We have a moral obligation to do so using principled, sound techniques."

Takeaways

  • Markov text generation and Metropolis posterior sampling are the same machinery: transition-only-on-current-state, implemented by reusing Markov<T>.
  • Continuous posteriors skip P(evidence): it's a constant factor, and Metropolis only needs weight quotients.
  • Metropolis does constant work per sample where rejection loops without bound.
  • The finale chains ch6's Choose, ch15's clamped prior, and ch13's Posterior: 9-of-10 heads moves belief to ~0.9.

CLOSING

The complete Fabulous.Collections

Sixteen chapters, one library. Everything above assembles into a single persistent data-structures project plus its demo applications — this tree is the digest's map of the book:

Chapter → artifact map.
ChaptersWhat lands in the library
1–2Persistence foundations: LinkedList, IImStack<out T>, ImQueue, UndoRedo, HList
3–4Depth & deduplication: finger-tree Deque; Memoizer + Quad (HashLife)
5–6Words & orderings: DAWG; Cartesian product, permutations, combinations, rank/unrank
8–10Developer tools: ImGraph + generic Backtracker; Doc pretty printer; unification/anti-unification
12–16The probability stack: distributions + alias method; ToJoint/Posterior; Bind (monad laws); continuous wing; Markov + Metropolis

If you read only five pages of the book, make them these: the Hughes-list reveal (figure 2.3 — a list that is a binary tree of closures); the finger tree emerging from overflowing end buffers (figure 3.5); the HashLife speed ladder (figure 4.12 — two ticks per level for the price of one); the exponential-to-linear unification result (figures 10.7–10.8 — HashLife's dedup in a new key); and the fairness posterior of the finale (chapter 16 — the whole book in one histogram).

Appendix A is the reading key for all that code: five C# features carry the entire fluent style — generics for the interfaces, extension methods for the combinators (the book's signature prior.ToJoint(likelihood).Filter(...).Project(...) reads "like a workflow"), lambdas for likelihoods, iterators for Samples(), and records/structs for the data — with the side-by-side note that C# instantiates generics at runtime where Java erases types and C++ templates macro-expand them. Appendix B is a further-reading list of the research papers behind each chapter — the same papers Lippert learned from.

All sample code lives at github.com/EricLippert/FabulousAdventures. And the closing moral stands on its own: software increasingly decides things about people, so "we have a moral obligation" to do it "using principled, sound techniques."

Takeaways

  • The book's arc — persistence → memoization → search → inference — is one library, sixteen files deep.
  • The recurring trick: make the state immutable and pure, then deduplicate, memoize, or sample it fearlessly.
